title: Biggest Lottery Winners in U.S. History: What Happened Next
description: From quitting jobs on the phone to winning $2 billion, America's biggest lottery winners reveal the hardest part isn't winning — it's what comes after.
content:
The Day Everything Changed

On the afternoon of August 23, 2017, Mavis Wanczyk did something most of us have only fantasized about. She picked up her phone and called her employer — Mercy Medical Center in Springfield, Massachusetts, where she had worked for 32 years — and told them she wasn't coming back. Not that day. Not ever. She had just matched all six numbers in the Powerball drawing and was now the sole winner of a $758.7 million jackpot, the largest ever won by a single ticket at that time. She didn't wait for a Monday morning meeting or a formal letter. She quit while the news was still sinking in.

That phone call — impulsive, joyful, disbelieving — is the kind of detail that cuts through the abstraction of nine-figure numbers. It makes the win feel real, human, and a little terrifying all at once. The stories of America's biggest lottery winners are full of moments like that: the first phone call, the first sleepless night, the first time someone they barely knew showed up asking for help. The money arrives in an instant. Everything else takes years.

Mavis Wanczyk — The Massachusetts Woman Who Walked Away

Mavis Wanczyk was 53 years old and working as a patient care associate when she bought her winning ticket at a Pride station in Chicopee, Massachusetts. She had picked some of her numbers based on family birthdays — a habit familiar to tens of millions of casual players. When she checked her ticket the morning after the August 23, 2017 drawing, she initially thought she'd matched five numbers. Then she saw the Powerball. Then she made that phone call.

At the press conference, Wanczyk was composed but visibly overwhelmed. She said she planned to "just go hide in [her] bed and snuggle" after claiming her prize. She chose the lump sum: approximately $480.5 million before taxes. After federal and Massachusetts state withholding, her take-home figure was significantly less — but still, by any measure, life-altering. She told reporters she intended to take care of her family and herself, and to do so quietly. She has largely kept that promise. Wanczyk has not been a fixture in tabloids or gossip columns. By all public accounts, she simply stepped out of one life and into another.

Life Before the Ticket — Who These Winners Were

What's striking about the biggest lottery winners in American history is how ordinary their lives were before the win. Mavis Wanczyk spent three decades caring for patients in a hospital. Gloria MacKenzie was 84 years old and living quietly in Zephyrhills, Florida when she claimed her $590.5 million Powerball jackpot in May 2013 — the largest ever won by a single ticket at that point, and MacKenzie became the oldest solo jackpot winner on record. She had reportedly let another shopper go ahead of her in line at the Publix where she bought the winning ticket. That stranger, in a small act of courtesy, changed nothing and everything.

Manuel Franco was 24 years old — barely out of his early twenties — when he won $768.4 million in Wisconsin in March 2019. Jack Whittaker was a construction company owner from Scott Depot, West Virginia, already a millionaire when he won $314.9 million on Christmas Day 2002. And Edwin Castro, the California man who claimed the largest lottery prize in world history — a staggering $2.04 billion Powerball jackpot drawn on November 8, 2022 — was a private individual whose life before the win was largely undocumented in the public record. The lump sum he chose came to approximately $997.6 million before taxes, the first time in U.S. lottery history that a single winner's cash option had crossed the $1 billion threshold.

The Moment After — Claims, Lawyers, and the First Decisions

Financial advisors consistently recommend that lottery winners do several things before claiming a major jackpot: retain a tax attorney, a financial planner, and an estate lawyer; consider whether to claim anonymously if the state allows it; and decide between the annuity and lump-sum options carefully. In practice, many winners — swept up in the moment — act quickly. Wanczyk claimed within days. Some winners, like Merle and Patricia Butler of Illinois, who won a share of the March 2012 Mega Millions jackpot, took a more measured approach and waited several months before coming forward.

The lump-sum versus annuity decision alone can shape the entire trajectory of a windfall. The annuity offers more money over time and enforced pacing; the lump sum offers control and immediacy, but requires disciplined management of a sum that few people — regardless of income history — have ever handled. Most big winners choose the lump sum. Most financial advisors caution that it comes with significant responsibility. The Most Surprising Thing a Winner Ever Said Publicly

"I just want to be left alone." — Mavis Wanczyk, at her August 2017 press conference, shortly after claiming the then-largest single-ticket Powerball jackpot in history.

That sentence landed differently than the typical winner's speech. No plans to buy a yacht. No announced charitable foundation. Just a 53-year-old woman from Massachusetts, blinking in the camera lights, saying out loud what might be the most honest thing any lottery winner has ever said publicly. She had just won nearly half a billion dollars. She wanted quiet. It's a small sentence that says something large about what money can and can't fix.

The Long Game — What the Money Did (and Didn't Do)

The long-term stories of major lottery winners are uneven, and the documented cases are sobering in their variety. Some of the most widely cited outcomes among big winners include:

  • Jack Whittaker, who won $314.9 million in West Virginia in 2002, faced a series of widely reported legal troubles, theft of hundreds of thousands of dollars from his car, and personal losses in the years following his win. His story is frequently cited in discussions about the psychological weight of sudden extreme wealth.
  • Gloria MacKenzie, at 84, claimed her $590.5 million Florida prize and subsequently faced a lawsuit from a woman who alleged she had been the one to allow MacKenzie to go ahead of her in line and use the Quick Pick terminal. The case was eventually dismissed, but it illustrated how quickly the legal world can find its way into a winner's life.
  • Mavis Wanczyk has, by all public accounts, managed to avoid the spotlight successfully — a rare and perhaps deliberate form of post-win success that gets less attention than the cautionary tales.
  • Multiple documented studies and journalistic investigations have noted that a significant percentage of large lottery winners report strained family relationships, an increase in unwanted contact from strangers and distant relatives, and in some cases, bankruptcy within five years of winning.

The pattern isn't universal, and it isn't inevitable. But it's consistent enough that financial professionals who work with sudden-wealth clients treat the first year after a major windfall as the most critical period — not for investment strategy, but for boundary-setting and emotional adjustment.

Lessons Without the Lecture — What These Stories Actually Teach Us

None of these winners asked to become case studies. They bought tickets, the numbers matched, and their lives changed in ways they couldn't have fully anticipated. What their stories collectively reveal isn't a formula or a warning so much as a portrait of human nature under pressure. Money at scale doesn't transform people — it amplifies what was already there. Wanczyk wanted peace and apparently found it. Whittaker wanted to give generously and did, even as other forces worked against him. MacKenzie wanted privacy and largely had it, until she didn't.

The biggest lottery winners in U.S. history all share one thing: they were ordinary people before the ticket, and they had to figure out how to remain people afterward. That turns out to be the harder problem.
